work.title: COMPARISON GUIDE
work.subtitle: A task-first option decision workbook
work.scope: Three fictional note-organising concepts, with assumed capabilities for teaching comparison. Not verified products, procurement advice, prices or market research.

pages.title: Start with the decision task.
pages.lead: Choose a way to keep working material understandable when you return to it. This guide compares three fictional approaches, not real competing products.
pages.body: Begin with the task and the constraints that would make an option unsuitable. The point is to expose trade-offs, not to manufacture a winner or imply that a larger feature count means greater value.
pages.detail: The comparison uses authored assumptions. Validate any real product capability and procurement requirement independently before adapting the guide.
pages.question: What must the chosen approach help the reader do?

records.label: Task
records.prompt: Return to material with enough context to use it.

records.label: Decision scope
records.prompt: Compare fictional organising approaches.

records.label: Non-goal
records.prompt: No ranking of actual vendors or products.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Turn needs into checkable criteria.
pages.lead: A useful criterion describes a task condition: keep an order, add a context note, or carry a small set of material without a network connection.
pages.body: Separate essential constraints from preferences. A reader may care more about portability than indexing, while another may need a clear review trail. Those differences should remain visible rather than disappear inside an unexplained score.
pages.detail: The guide supplies four binary assumptions for illustration. It does not assign importance on behalf of a buyer or claim that the assumptions are verified.
pages.question: Which requirement would rule out an otherwise appealing option?

records.label: Essential
records.prompt: Define the task condition that cannot be compromised.

records.label: Preference
records.prompt: Record a benefit that may be traded off.

records.label: Unknown
records.prompt: Check requirements that the current model does not address.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Use the same comparison rules.
pages.lead: The three concepts are a sequence folio, a context-card box and a review binder. Each is described using the same four capability assumptions.
pages.body: A yes means assumed present in this fictional model; a no means assumed absent. Neither means independently tested, universally available or unsuitable for every reader. Unknown real-world facts must not be silently converted into no.
pages.detail: The four dimensions are sequence, context note, portable set and review trail. They are not a comprehensive product specification.
pages.question: Would another reviewer interpret each flag the same way?

records.label: Yes
records.prompt: Assumed present in this illustrative concept.

records.label: No
records.prompt: Assumed absent, not a verified product limitation.

records.label: Unknown real fact
records.prompt: Requires checking; do not replace it with a model flag.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Describe the options in plain language.
pages.lead: The sequence folio keeps material in an intended order. The context-card box emphasises a question beside a note. The review binder keeps a structured review trail.
pages.body: These are design concepts, not offers for sale. Their descriptions explain a comparison lens without implying construction quality, security, support or compatibility.
pages.detail: A useful description helps the reader picture the task. Keep promotional superlatives out of a guide that is meant to support a considered choice.
pages.question: Which organising priority matches the task rather than the headline?

records.label: Sequence folio
records.prompt: Ordered material with a portable set.

records.label: Context-card box
records.prompt: Context notes with a portable set.

records.label: Review binder
records.prompt: Ordered material, context notes and a review trail.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Read the matrix without a score.
pages.lead: The fictional matrix contains eight yes flags across twelve cells. The total describes the model only; it is not a quality rating or a market statistic.
pages.body: Sequence folio has sequence, portable set and review trail. Context-card box has context note and portable set. Review binder has sequence, context note and review trail, but not portable set. These are authored assumptions, not tested product capabilities.
pages.detail: Check source CSV or JSON for every flag. Do not add a feature to the narrative without changing the source register and rebuilding the guide.
pages.question: Which individual flag matters to this reader’s task?

records.prompt: Context note and portable set assumed.

records.prompt: Sequence, context note and review trail assumed.

pages.title: Match a scenario before recommending.
pages.lead: For a person carrying a small set of references, portability may matter first. For a person explaining why a passage was saved, a context note may matter more.
pages.body: The scenarios show how priorities change the conversation. They do not establish a universally best option. A real recommendation needs actual constraints, verified capabilities and the reader’s informed judgement.
pages.detail: Use a scenario to ask what would happen in practice. If two options remain plausible, identify the smallest appropriate comparison activity.
pages.question: Which scenario is closest to the actual task?

records.label: Carry a small set
records.prompt: Check the portable-set assumption first.

records.prompt: Check the context-note assumption first.

records.prompt: Check sequence and review-trail assumptions together.

pages.title: Treat cost as an unanswered question.
pages.lead: No prices, implementation effort or support conditions are supplied. A lower apparent purchase price would not by itself establish lower total cost.
pages.body: Ask about setup, maintenance, storage, accessibility and the work of changing an existing practice. Keep monetary amounts unknown until an appropriate, current source supports them.
pages.detail: The source model contains capabilities only. It cannot justify an affordability claim, a savings figure or a procurement budget.
pages.question: Which ongoing responsibility could change the cost conversation?

records.label: Purchase terms
records.prompt: No price or commercial offer supplied.

records.label: Ongoing effort
records.prompt: Setup and maintenance need investigation.

records.label: Comparison boundary
records.prompt: Capability flags do not establish total cost.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Make omissions visible.
pages.lead: The model says nothing about durability, privacy, accessibility or specialist requirements. Those omissions may matter more than the four displayed dimensions.
pages.body: A comparison guide should tell a reader what it does not cover. Do not use a neat matrix to imply a complete assessment, certification or suitability decision.
pages.detail: If an omitted condition is essential, pause the choice and obtain the relevant information. A blank in the evidence is not permission to assume a favourable answer.
pages.question: Which missing dimension should prevent a decision today?

records.label: Unassessed
records.prompt: Durability and accessibility are not evaluated.

records.label: Unverified
records.prompt: No actual product, vendor or test result supplied.

records.label: Pause condition
records.prompt: An essential requirement lacks appropriate evidence.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Write a provisional choice record.
pages.lead: A good decision record states the task, the option considered and the unresolved condition that could change the choice. It need not pretend certainty.
pages.body: Use the three fields below as a working decision note. The example favours no real product and does not replace organisational procurement, specialist review or a buyer’s own evaluation.
pages.subheading: A choice that can be revisited
pages.detail: Keep the evidence version with the record. If an assumed capability changes, revisit the reasoning rather than preserving the old conclusion for consistency.
pages.question: What new fact would cause this provisional choice to change?

records.label: Task condition
records.prompt: A portable set is essential for this scenario.

records.label: Options to inspect
records.prompt: Sequence folio and context-card box remain plausible.

records.label: Open condition
records.prompt: Verify actual context and review requirements.

evidenceRows: 3 concepts × 4 flags / 8 yes cells / not verified products.

pages.title: Ask for the missing information.
pages.lead: Before committing, ask a provider or maker to demonstrate the exact task and explain the limits of the proposed option. Request current, attributable information.
pages.body: This guide supplies no live consultation destination or purchasing service. Use its questions to structure a real evaluation, and preserve the distinction between an authored model and verified product evidence.
pages.detail: A useful enquiry describes the task and the unresolved criterion. Avoid asking only whether an option is best, because the comparison has not defined a universal winner.
pages.question: What demonstration would reduce the most important uncertainty?

records.label: Question to send
records.prompt: Show how the option handles this specific task.

records.label: Evidence to request
records.prompt: Current capability information and relevant conditions.

records.prompt: No purchase or procurement approval established.
